messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Prior for degrees of freedom
parts:
Do we have any recommendations for priors for student_t's degrees of freedom parameter? 

I was looking in the manual and searching through stan-users but didn't really find anything, although maybe I missed something. If I remember correctly there's a recommendation in ARM for uniform on 1/df, but I think that might have been to deal with a BUGS-related issue.

messages.author: a236d3d356ca53fd
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Prior for degrees of freedom
parts:
I recommend as an easy default option
 nu ~ gamma(2,0.1); 

This was proposed and anlysed by Juárez and Steel (2010) (Model-based clustering of non-Gaussian panel data based on skew-t distributions. Journal of Business & Economic Statistics 28, 52–66.). Juárez and Steel compere this to Jeffreys prior and report that the difference is small.  Simpson et al (2014) (arXiv:1403.4630) propose a theoretically well justified "penalised complexity (PC) prior", which they show to have a good behavior for the degrees of freedom, too. PC prior might be the best choice, but requires numerical computation of the prior (which could computed in a grid and interpolated etc.). It would be feasible to implement it in Stan, but it would require some work. Unfortunately no-one has compared PC prior and this gamma prior directly, but based on the discussion with Daniel Simpson, although PC prior would be better this gamma(2,0.1) prior is not a bad choice. Thus, I would use it until someone implements the PC prior for degrees of freedom of the Student's t in Stan.

Aki

messages.author: 146bc26797d1c5e2
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Prior for degrees of freedom
parts:
That df+1: at least in earlier versions of Stan, one could have a half-normal but not an artificially truncated normal. I guess it is possible now, but I've stuck to the old habit...

Maybe the prior reflects my prior knowledge. :) Usually there is no reason to assume accurate gaussianity in our applications. I'm not particularly interested in getting the df's or observed variance inferred right. The motivation for t distribution is just to dampen the influence of outliers.

Also my impression has been that the t distribution becomes quite Gaussian around df ≈ 30.  The differences are then mainly further away in the tails, at densities that are astronomically small anyway. But may that isn't so. (I haven't read the papers.)

Then there is the geometry of the parameter space. If in terms of data df≈30 and df≈300 give about the same likelihood, the posterior of the df is long-tailed itself and maybe hard to sample.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Prior for degrees of freedom
parts:
> On Mar 7, 2015, at 3:28 AM, Janne Sinkkonen <janne.s...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> That df+1: at least in earlier versions of Stan, one could have a half-normal but not an artificially truncated normal. I guess it is possible now, but I've stuck to the old habit...

We actually had arbitrary truncation in version 1, not that
it matters. All you ever needed is:

parameters {
real<lower=1> nu;

model {
nu ~ normal(...);

Because we only need the log prob function up to an additive
constant, you don't even need to use truncation in the normal.

- Bob
